Why more brands are paying creators to make their ads

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
  • This article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most important information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics.
  • Brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

This article is part of an ongoing series detailing the most important information readers need to know about the ad industry’s most complex topics. More from the series →.

Brands paying influencers to make campaign creative have become key drivers of investment in the booming creator economy. Creative agencies might want to take note.

Sources indicate that “You get the authentic, scroll-stopping content that people want to engage each with. But you also get the reach,” said Katy Ball, head of social at M&C Saatchi Sport & Entertainment.

As spending on paid social channels — and video in particular — continues to rise, demand for creative assets to appear in those ad slots is increasing.

Recent findings suggest that the number of assets attached to individual campaigns has risen 30% in the last five years, according to a CreativeX study of 115,990 ad campaigns, representing $11 billion in ad spend. Per the study, just five assets receive 88% of media investment in an average campaign.

The need for more campaign assets is fueling the growth of asset-led spending, the fastest growing segment of the creator economy, according to a report published this week by research consultancy Madison & Wall.

Sources indicate that at the moment, 12% of the $112 billion spent on creators globally goes towards creators producing ads on behalf of brands, per the study. That’s expected to rise 16% every year through 2030.

The days when brands principally paid creators to rent their following are rapidly disappearing. Influencers are now media partners, ambassadors and increasingly, cogs in the creative production supply chain. And brands see creator-made ads as a solution to their social asset shortage.

“For us, the appeal is simple. Buying space in someone’s feed doesn’t mean you’ve earned their attention. Good creators understand what their audiences care about and how to give them something worth stopping for,” said Jared Kozel, co-founder and chief creative officer at agency Super Nice. “That’s valuable creative judgment to bring into an ad no matter the brand or category.”.

Influencer marketing experts note that several different but related practices are included under the broader umbrella of creator-led production.

While some brands simply pay creators a fee in order to receive video or still assets for use in a campaign, whitelisting (also called “dark advertising”) has become a favored method of managing such arrangements.

In this context, an influencer grants a brand limited access to their social media accounts, allowing them to book a paid media campaign through that account, using assets made by the creator while taking advantage of discrete audience targeting.

“What we’re seeing is a lot of recutting of media spend to be allocated towards creator development in order to fund whitelisting,” remarked Olivia Wedderburn, head of influence at Born Social.

Madison & Wall’s research suggested that funding for creative production may also be coming from PR, social or experimental budgets, as well as traditional media or production pots of money.

Another related practice, user generated content, sees brands paying regular social media people to license their content as creative assets in ad campaigns.

“They have to feed their their content engines, and they’re opening up as many different avenues as they can,” remarked Andy Ryan, co-founder at social and influencer agency Komodo.

The relative low cost of working with influencers, versus creative production agencies, is the primary driver behind brand spending on creator-made assets.

Although production spending is often a small fraction of an overall campaign budget, marketers are keen to squeeze every non-working (that is, non-media) dollar for all it’s worth. While that same desire is pushing some brands toward generative AI production techniques, others are turning to creators.

According to recent reports, but as this type of spending grows, so to does the need to manage it effectively. “It’s never been more complicated to negotiate usage rights or exclusivity,” said Wedderburn.

Billion Dollar Boy, for example, recently added features to its Companion creator management tool designed to better facilitate creator-led production efforts and manage usage rights negotiations.

“The creator economy has never been more competitive, heightening the urgency for brands to understand the market context,” stated Thomas Walters, the agency’s chief innocation officer and co-founder.

At the same time, increased brand spending in this area is already leading to an uptick in the fees commanded by some creators. Last year, agency practitioners reported creator rates ticking up 10-20% due to demand for expanded rights.

There’s also some evidence to show that creator-made assets perform as well as, or even better than, traditional advertising spots in a social context.

A report by System1, WPP Media and Goat published in June found that creator ads achieved 3.2X the brand-awareness lift for category leader ads as traditional advertising creative.

“We’re seeing a lot of brands say that is more valuable in terms of conversion and reach than some of the quick-and-dirty assets they previously would have relied on,” noted Wedderburn.

Sources indicate that that’s not unexpected. Audiences recognize the visual cues, language and production methods employed by creators as native to TikTok or Instagram, while clocking films shot on a closed set or using more traditional methods as foreign that same environment, a lesson that major advertisers like Nike are reluctantly absorbing.

It has been revealed that “If programs are set up correctly, creators can deliver volume and variety faster and more cost effectively than a traditional production cycle,” said Nicholas Spiro, chief commercial officer, Viral Nation. “The shift we’re seeing is brands starting to plan creators across their media budgets, rather than as a separate influencer line item alone.”.

Consulting giants Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

With shareholders, an $895 billion compute bill and a costly free tier, Anthropic’s no-ads pledge may have a shelf life.

    Anthropic says no to ads but Wall Street may have other ideas

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • Anthropic is a public company now, which puts it on an unofficial path to an ads business.
    • It has been revealed that unofficial because the company’s official position is still firmly against ads.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Anthropic is a public company now, which puts it on an unofficial path to an ads business.

    It has been revealed that unofficial because the company’s official position is still firmly against ads. It went as far as spending Super Bowl money on a campaign mocking OpenAI for bringing them to ChatGPT. Its prospectus, the document pitching those public shares to investors, leaves advertisers out of the business altogether.

    Recent findings suggest that “Is it cynical to expect Anthropic to follow the same route? Not really. More like an educated guess,” remarked ad tech expert Shirley Marschall.

    Besides, the tech giant has already left the door open, she continued. Its pledge rules out sponsored links adjacent to conversations, but in the same post it claims it will keep building features that help people “find, compare, or buy products, connect with businesses.” And once an agent recommends products, retail media will pay to be in those recommendations, Marschall stated, before adding: “Let’s see Anthropic turn that ad revenue down,” she added.

    Advertisers, for their part, will be watching closely, and with mixed feelings. On the one hand, a fresh media seller means a new platform to wrangle and one more set of tools and teams to learn at a time when most are still working out how to buy ChatGPT. On the other hand, Claude’s audience is also spending more and more time in those conversation threads. For marketers, that’s a hard place to stay out of for long.

    “Anthropic, like any organization, has a stance towards handling consumer data and inadvertently how advertising is considered,” remarked independent ad tech consultant Jonathan D’Souza Rauto. “But monetization is a lucrative form of revenue. I’d expect Anthropic to have a change of heart. Look no further to how Apple has played this advertising game over the past few years despite being considered anti-advertising.”.

    Life as a public firm isn’t cheap, after all, and it’s even less cheap for an AI company that has signed up for approximately $895.4 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, some running to 2045. That’s more than 13 years of revenue at its current pace, given Q3 revenue of $17 billion. The revenue covering that bill is far less locked in since 80% of revenue is consumption-based and the S-1 indicates many customers can cut usage or terminate on short notice. In fact, the company has already warned that “operating margins may compress when large tranches arrive.”.

    It has been revealed that then there’s the free tier. “Free and promotional people may never convert to paid looks,” the filing admits, yet Anthropic still pays to serve every one of them. Analysts found that cost sits in sales and marketing out of sight of the headline margin. That arrangement holds as long as free users keep upgrading. If they stop, Anthropic is left with a growing audience it pays to serve and earns nothing from.

    OpenAI has already shown what that audience could be worth. ChatGPT ads reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launching. When both companies are trading, analysts will ask Anthropic why it’s leaving money on the table.

    In a recent development, “They’ll go after advertising, just not in the way some assume,” stated Rob Webster, founder and CEO of TAU Marketing Solutions. “The prize for Anthropic isn’t ads inside Claude. Advertising is now a trillion-dollar market, and the real power sits with whatever brain coordinates it: deciding what runs, where, and why. That’s a far more valuable position than selling impressions. Anthropic wants to be a fresh, better Microsoft or Apple. Selling tools to businesses. Not ad opportunities.”.

    There are reasons, though, why Anthropic may resist the lure of ads for as long as it feasibly can.

    According to recent reports, “Trust and impartiality really matter with LLMs, particularly among enterprise customers,” said Alex Tait, founder of Entropy. “In contrast to OpenAI, Anthropic is currently approaching operating break-even without ads suggesting its existing business model could be commercially sustainable without it.”.

    Anthropic’s anti-ads stance is based on its perspective that once ads become part of a business’s revenue targets, the pressure to maximize engagement can start influencing product decisions. For an AI app, in this case Claude, that creates a conflict: people expect Claude to help them make decisions in their own interests, not towards whatever generates revenue for the manufacturer or its advertisers. And in its IPO prospectus, the company said that they want “Claude’s only incentive to be giving them [users] a helpful answer,” which is why they have “chosen not to introduce that pressure [ads] into Claude.”.

    Anthropic did not respond to Digiday’s request for comment.

    Tech Report: Future of Marketing Briefing: Consulting firms revive their marketing ambitions in the C-suite the holdcos covet

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • It has been revealed that this Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m.
    • However the holdcos settle the question of whether the CEO route counts as due diligence, Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song got there first, and both have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    It has been revealed that this Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    However the holdcos settle the question of whether the CEO route counts as due diligence, Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song got there first, and both have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

    Industry observers note that deloitte Digital’s offer is Converge, an operating system that strings together AI agents to run marketing and sales work, from research and briefs through to campaign deployment and deal tracking. Some of the agents are Deloitte’s own. Others are ones a client already runs elsewhere, and the whole thing plugs into the tools and clout contracts a brand is already paying for. Marketing and sales versions are live, with commerce on the way, and Deloitte pitches them as one front-office system tied to revenue, which it calls “brand to cash.” Because it’s sold as a license that stretches across sales, marketing and service, it needs sign-off well above the CMO, which suits a consulting firm that’s used to having those conversations.

    Accenture Song’s play in media, a market it has circled in the U.S. for years without committing. In September, it moved Melissa Fein, who built its media planning and buying business in Australia and Fresh Zealand after leaving Initiative in 2024, to New York as U.S. media lead. This month it posted a job for a head of media strategy for the Americas. The ad describes a “new world media practice” with no legacy systems to protect, and asks for an AI-first strategist” to lead planning, build new tools and become the person senior clients call before a brief exists.

    In a recent development, candidates need hands-on command of econometrics, incrementality testing and attribution plus experience in substantial-spending categories like financial services, telecommunications, automotive and health. Those are the categories where the ANZ team won Australia Post and Mediabank. Accenture Song Ndidi Oteh has kept quiet on specifics, saying only that whatever it does in media won’t take traditional forms.

    Sources indicate that “The real prize is the conversation before the brief,” said  Steve Boehler, founder of agency consultancy the Mercer Island Group. ”If you help define the business problem, design the operating model and decide how success will be measured, you are competing long before an agency review begins.”.

    Industry observers note that both plays echo what the holdcos have spent 18 months engineering: operating systems that run a client’s marketing for it and media businesses that sell more than buying. The consultants may have the better shot at making either one stick. They already sit with the CEOs, CIOs and CFOs who sign off on systems spanning sales, marketing and service and installing that kind of software is their day job. A holdco operating system, rightly or wrongly, still reads as an agency tool, built partly to make the agency cheaper to run. Accenture also arrives in the U.S. media with no legacy buying business to protect, so it can lead with measurement and tools before it has to sell buying power.

    Whether any of this translates is another matter. Consultancies have been trying to crack advertising for the best part of a decade, after all, and the media buying business still rewards a scale Accenture doesn’t yet have in the U.S. Then again, now is arguably as good a time as any for them to try, if not better. With Omnicom and IPG combined, major advertisers are down to three holdcos, and some are skipping the pitch one so a credible alternative has rarely been more useful. AI is also pushing decisions about how marketing works into rooms where the CFO and CIO sit, which consultancies have been in for years. And a C-suite that takes a closer look at marketing will start asking how agencies make their money, from data fees to principal media, which is an awkward question for any firm with a buying business to defend.

    It has been revealed that “The consultancies may have an advantage in getting invited to design the system,” stated Boehler. “That is not the same as proving they can run marketing better. The client still needs evidence of better decisions, better work and better business outcomes, not just fewer handoffs.”.

    According to recent reports, all of which makes the Publicis-WPP episode look a little quaint, partly because it was never quite the fight it was billed as. Sadoun spent months telling investors that Publicis was winning big accounts without a pitch. Rose, asked about it by an analyst, called it “this pitchless CEO handshake thing that I keep getting asked about” and mentioned decisions that big deserve careful consideration. Publicis answered with an open letter treating that line as her theory, and the coverage did the rest. Somewhere along the way, a question about how clients choose agencies turned into a row about manners.

    According to recent reports, what got lost was the shift both CEOs were describing. Big advertisers are increasingly buying data, identity and AI infrastructure, which a six-week parade of slide decks was never built to judge, so some now test one partner in depth instead of auditioning several. Those decisions are also moving up the organization chart, to executives who sign off on systems not campaigns. That’s how consultancies have always been bought. Deloitte and Accenture are built for long, technical evaluations run by CFOs and CIOs, and while the holdcos; remarks were being turned into a grudge march one launched a system that needs the c-suite’s signature and the other started building a U.S. media practice designed to win it.

    Industry observers note that “Client CEOs and CMOs pay attention to CEOs of holdcos, especially when a transition in agency leadership occurs and the agency CEO conducts outreach to key clients,” stated Gartner analyst Jay Wilson. “But most recognize that while agency CEOs may set a direction for the agency, that direction may be slow to take hold – or never take hold – within the agency teams doing the actual day-to- day work. A strong relationship with, or aversion to, an agency chief executive is usually more consequential at smaller, independent agencies.”.

    Whatever gets agreed in the c-suite, someone still has to do the work.

    “The consultants don’t have to copy the incumbent model to compete,” stated Boehler. “But they still have to do the work: blueprint, negotiate, deliver, reconcile and prove results. A different model is a proposition until clients experience the difference.”.

    Sources indicate that cinema admissions have climbed back on the strength of a fuller blockbuster slate and much of the ad money that shifted to digital during lockdowns stayed put. Most screens still sell their preshow through sales houses that have always sold offline.

    Mikkel Hagedorn, a WPP and Omnicom alum, has spent five or six years building a platform that lets buyers book cinema spots programmatically, target them against specific films and count impressions straight off ticket sales. The tech giant is live in Denmark and Finland, where sales houses have handed it two minutes of a 15-minute preshow at a base CPM of around €75. Hagedorn’s bet is that exhibitors can bring cinema into the digital ad market while keeping the premium pricing newspapers gave away when they went programmatic.

    His organization, called Cinemataztic, gives buyers two ways to purchase inventory: first, agencies already running programmatic campaigns can reach the inventory through supply-side platforms and demand-side platforms such as Smartclip Google’s DV360 respectively, which lets cinema sit inside budgets that were going to be spread across other channels anyway, Advertisers who would rather skip the intermediary fees can book directly through Hagedorn’s own interface.

    Either way, the buyer can pick what individual film they want to target, so a brand could run only against the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday movie if it likes. The impressions they buy come straight from exhibitors’ ticketing systems, which means one ticket sold counts as one impression. There are “no multipliers here,” said Hagedorn, a dig at the audience multipliers that inflate numbers elsewhere in media.

    Industry observers note that so far a lot of the money has come from digital agencies edging up the funnel into brand work. Hagedorn stated he has seen little cannibalisation of advertisers still buying cinema the old way. He said the business has grown 50% a year and forecasts the same for next year, when the tech giant expands into Sweden, Thailand and a third, bigger market he wouldn’t share.

    Even so, the programmatication of cinema will be a slow burn. Advertising is still its third-largest revenue line after tickets and concessions. Most hand it entirely to sales houses on contracts of three to five years and only learn that demand is falling when the next guarantee shrinks. Hagedorn has been warning them about this for years. “They cannot stay offline forever,” he mentioned.

    Sources indicate that brands that gatecrash cultural moments tend to stick to tournaments and royal weddings, and they rarely pick a game that lets players mug strangers in a fake Florida. Grand Theft Auto, the culture-warping franchise, is the exception, and its sixth installment is drawing the kind of guerilla marketing normally reserved for FIFA and the Olympics.

    Anyone trying to keep up can follow the running tally at GTA6Brands.com, an independent tracker run by Mike Litman that logs a fresh stunt each day for his GTA 6 Marketing News podcast. Hardly anything in culture still sets off that kind of scramble across so many brands at once, and with GTA the explanation is scale.

    “I’ve tracked over 290 brand moves around GTA 6 so far, including around 130 unofficial activations,” said Litman. “That’s a remarkable amount of marketing activity orbiting a product launch, particularly when so many of those brands have no formal relationship with Rockstar. What’s interesting is the range of brands getting involved.”.

    It has been revealed that with media this fragmented, marketers have a shortlist of moments when a mass audience shows up at the same time, and most of those moments involve a ball. GTA earned its spot on that list over 13 years. When GTA 5 launched in 2013 it made $1 billion in three days, which owner Take Two called a rate faster than any other video game, film or other entertainment product has ever managed. For context, Marvel’s “The Avengers” movie took 19 days to reach that number. In the years since it launched, the game has since surpassed 230 million units sold worldwide across three console generations. The wait for the sequel turned into an event of its own. GTA 6’s second trailer received 475 million views across all platforms within 24 hours of its release, beating the 365 million in 24 hours for Marvel’s Deadpool & Wolverine film. Take Two has issued $8 billion for its 2027 guidance for the fiscal year the game launches in. For a brand that wants a crowd all watching the same thing at once, that’s about as close to a World Cup final as entertainment gets, and nobody has to get past FIFA’s lawyers.

    In a recent development, “I think the fascinating thing is that GTA 6 has achieved something usually reserved for the World Cup or Super Bowl, but without the stadium, the broadcast rights or the traditional sponsorship machinery,” said Litman. “It’s become a cultural event in its own right. And brands aren’t waiting for permission to participate.”.

    Sources indicate that A few did get permission, though. Rockstar’s list of official partners is short and made up mostly of platforms. Sony signed an exclusive marketing deal, which put a “Plays Best on PS5” tag on the game’s official channels. Netflix got the “Extended Look” trailer six trailers before YouTube in August, in what Take Two boss Strauss Zelnick called a “groundbreaking partnership”. YouTube is running a 24-hour launch live livestream from its own channel, and the Miami Heat have redesigned court, custom uniforms and Vice City merchandise.

    According to recent reports, “Nike is going back to its roots and what built the brand: cultural relevance through people who have the trust of a community. It is a bold choice when most advertising pitches are about AI. Nike uses AI too, as a tool, but clearly demonstrates it understands that what stays scarce is trust. Trust comes from identity and proximity: who is speaking, and how close they are to the community listening. It also shows what creators and athletes must build to ask a brand like Nike for more than just a campaign fee. Most of them are offering access to an audience that belongs to a social or tech platform, targeted and measured with the data that the platform makes available. Global stars aside, only those who directly own the relationship with their audience and their data can negotiate a share of the long-term value.”.

    — Alessandro De Zanche, founder of media consultancy ADZ Strategies on Nike’s bet on creators to drive growth.

    $70.7 million: The total amount that U.S. advertisers spent on ChatGPT ads during October.

    $83: The initial share price for Anthropic when the company went public.

    $24.6 billion: The total that U.S. B2B digital ad spend is expected to reach by the end of 2026.

    $1.65 billion: Total in pre-order sales ahead of the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 launch.

    Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing consumers’ photosItaly has fined Meta €805m for scanning about 20 million Android users’ Facebook photo galleries without proper consent, and Meta plans to appeal, according to the BBC.

    Meta Testing Latest Prediction-Market App With EmployeesMeta staff are testing Takes, an internal prediction-market app where people bet points called “cred” instead of real money, and there’s no word yet on a public launch, per The Wall Street Journal.

    Inside YouTube’s Co-View PolicyYouTube now adds an estimated number of viewers watching on TVs to public view counts, based on a statistical model rather than device monitoring, though this doesn’t change creator payouts, according to The Publish Press.

    TikTok Outpaces Instagram on Brand Engagement Despite Equal Reach, Report FindsA Dash Social report finds that brand posts on TikTok and Instagram reach roughly the same audience, but TikTok earns a higher engagement rate by views (3.9% versus Instagram’s 2.6%), per Net Influencer.

    Substack job listing hints at a bigger advertising push in 2027Substack’s upcoming payments job listing includes exploring ads around 2027, a clear change from its earlier “distant future” line on advertising.

    In Graphic Detail: Welcome to the agentic commerce quarterHoliday 2026 is shaping up as the first season in which AI shopping agents actually complete purchases, though it’s still early: only 31% of consumers say they’re likely to let an agent buy without reviewing the purchase first.

    Mail Metro Media’s next creator play is representing them Mail Metro Media, the Daily Mail’s ad sales arm, is building an in-house talent agency to represent its creators, which raises an obvious conflict between selling audiences to brands and getting the best deals for the talent.

    Inside Nike’s blueprint to turn creators into brand buildersNike noted it will give creators, local cultural voices, and everyday participants a larger role in building its brand, moving beyond major campaigns and superstar deals.

    With shareholders, an $895 billion compute bill and a costly free tier, Anthropic’s no-ads pledge may have a shelf life.

    Creator-led production is the fastest-growing segment of the influencer economy. We explain what’s driving investment in this practice.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • What if your next playground was to build a global, iconic Brand, with a creative machine that never sleeps, and compounds?
    • It has been revealed that we’re not looking for a "Social Media Manager" to follow a calendar.
    • Someone who understands that to win today, you don’t just need "content", you need a Movement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What if your next playground was to build a global, iconic Brand, with a creative machine that never sleeps, and compounds?

    It has been revealed that we’re not looking for a "Social Media Manager" to follow a calendar. We’re looking for an AI-native Creative Director (Brand & Content).

    Someone who understands that to win today, you don’t just need "content", you need a Movement.

    According to recent reports, this isn’t another content job. Most content teams use AI to write captions faster. That’s the 99%. We want to be in the 0.1%: a media where AI runs the creative loop, from the signal to the hook, the cut, the post and the lesson. Every day, on every platform, in French and in English. You bring the taste. The machine you build brings the scale.

    Industry observers note that here’s the bet: a company that learns by itself grows in a way a company of people alone can’t. We aim for $10M in revenue with 10 people, each of them running a dozen agents.

    Sources indicate that paradoxically, the more AI runs our content, the more human it has to feel. AI doesn’t make more of what everyone makes. It makes more of what only we can make.

    Our creative machine has to be able to:.

    1. Read the signals. Comments, DMs, retention graphs, saves, shares, search trends, objections from sales calls, and what the best creators and advertisers in the world are publishing right now.

    Recent findings suggest that 2. Hold the full context of Paradox. Our DNA, years of interviews, lives and courses, member stories, and every past post with what it taught us, in one shared firm brain.

    Sources indicate that 3. Generate in our voice. Hooks, scripts, shorts, carousels, cuts, thumbnails and captions, in French and in English.

    In a recent development, 4. Ship. Format, schedule, publish and answer, on every platform.

    5. Measure with real KPIs. Retention, shares, saves, follower growth, and the followers who become leads and members. Not likes.

    In a recent development, 6. Learn and loop on its own. Double down on what works, kill what doesn’t, write the lesson back into the brain, and start the next cycle without waiting for a meeting.

    This is already real. An ads library of thousands of creatives feeds our creative research. Agents cut ads from long-form content and wire Instagram comment-to-DM automations. And our product is AI-native too: Athena, our AI coach, works with members every day.

    At Paradox, we are convinced that greatness is trainable, and we believe self-help is broken.

    Most learning platforms are used the same way: consuming generic theories, getting quick highs, ending with no real change.

    People deserve more: a system that knows them, one that adapts, challenges, and grows with them.

    That’s why we want to empower people at scale, by leveraging cutting edge technologies like AI, and crafting user experiences with outstanding aesthetics.

    - Human Intelligence (coaches, peers, and mentors).

    - Structured Intelligence (protocols, mental models, rituals).

    - Technological Intelligence (AI personalization, feedback loops, adaptive journeys).

    To create one seamless ecosystem: Paradox OS.

    It has been revealed that paradox was founded by David Laroche, a creator followed by over 2 million people and known for his interviews with icons like Tony Parker, Mike Horn, Richard Branson and Gad Elmaleh. We started in French. We’re building for the world.

    You lead the Content Factory not by management, but with creativity.

    In a classic content team, people do the work and AI helps. Here it’s the other way round: agents do the volume, you design the machine, set the bar and make the calls. Humans do what no machine can: taste.

    Build a symbiotic strategy where David Laroche’s personal brand and Paradox’s firm brand reinforce each other without cannibalization.

    Implement radical new formats (documentaries, conceptual shorts) that shatter the boring codes of the "Self-Help" industry.

    Define distinct, sharp editorial lines for each platform: Depth & Search for YouTube, Aesthetic & Vibe for Instagram, and Authority & Authenticity for LinkedIn.

    ❌ The old way: a strategy deck written once a year, and a calendar filled by habit.

    According to recent reports, 🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: agents watch every platform, every competitor and every comment continuously. They tell you which angle is rising, which format is tiring and which story our audience asks for. The strategy updates every week, on evidence.

    Take responsibility for the entire production chain from hooks to storyboarding the narrative, and ensuring the final cut matches the vision.

    Own the packaging: titles, thumbnails and the first 3 seconds. You test variants every week and know your click-through and retention numbers by heart.

    ❌ The old way: one shoot becomes one video and a handful of posts.

    🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: one shoot, one live or one interview becomes dozens of hooks, shorts, carousels and ad cuts by the next morning, in both languages. Concepts are tested with AI-generated drafts before we spend a day shooting them.

    Your taste becomes the eval. You write down what makes a great hook, a great cut, a great carousel and a great story, in rules and examples the agents check themselves against. Each time you reject something, the reason goes back into the rules.

    Act as the final quality check: nothing gets published if it doesn’t meet the "Paradox Standard" of aesthetics and storytelling, whether a person or an agent made it.

    ❌ The old way: a creative team briefs an editor, waits three days and gets two versions.

    🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: agents draft, cut, caption, translate and schedule. You keep the best, and next week their first drafts are already closer to your bar.

    Analyze retention graphs, CTR, and CPL to iterate based on feedback, killing what fails and aggressively scaling what works.

    ❌ The old way: someone pulls the stats at the end of the month and nobody changes anything.

    🏴‍☠️ At Paradox: agents read the numbers of every post every day, explain why it worked or didn’t, and propose the next test. You measure the machine itself: posts per week, time from idea to live, hit rate, and the share of the work done without a human.

    We started in French. You build the machine that takes Paradox to English-speaking audiences: channels, formats and voice that feel native, not translated.

    And always: real stories told with consent, no fake claims, no fake scarcity. The machine can scale, but it doesn’t decide what’s right. You do.

    It has been revealed that how you’ll know you’re AI-native: you spend your time on concepts, taste and calls, not on resizing, captioning and exporting. The output grows every month while the team doesn’t.

    Industry observers note that proven Content Builder: You have successfully grown a media brand, a YouTube channel, or a personal brand to significant scale (100k+ followers or millions of views). You understand the mechanics of virality and retention. You’ve created at least one format that broke out, and you can show its click-through and retention numbers.

    It has been revealed that elite Scripting Skills: You can show us scripts you wrote that performed. You know how to structure a narrative, write a hook that stops the scroll, and keep an audience engaged for 20+ minutes.

    Performance Fluency: You have worked in environments where content had to drive business results (ads, debuts, conversion), not just vanity metrics.

    Sources indicate that AI-native Creative: you’ve built content pipelines with AI yourself: Claude Code, automations, generative video, image and voice tools, evals. Show us something you built, not a certificate.

    Industry observers note that intolerant to Mediocrity: You have "Taste." You are physically pained by a bad font, a clumsy cut, or a weak headline. You fight for the details that others ignore, including in what AI produces.

    Recent findings suggest that psychology Obsessed: You don’t just "make content"; you study human nature. You constantly ask why people click, why they share, and what emotion drives them.

    Sources indicate that A "Doer" with Authority: You command respect not by title, but by competence. You can jump into a project, write the script, direct the shoot, and fix the edit if needed.

    Loop thinker: you see every platform as a loop that can learn, and you can’t stop yourself from closing it.

    No Ego, Just Impact: You don’t fall in love with your ideas. You accept that even the best concepts can flop. When it happens, you don’t take it personally; you analyze the data, pivot immediately, and ship the next concept with renewed energy.

    English: Fluent English, you can hold a conversation on specific details with English-speaking colleagues.

    Our chosen language for written communication is English.

    ❌ If you need clarity before chaos: wrong place.

    ❌ If you prefer balance over intensity: wrong season.

    ❌ If you don’t genuinely care about the topics we cover: wrong place.

    ❌ If you want to strategize without getting your hands dirty in scripting, directing, or the editing suite: wrong role.

    ❌ If you think AI content means generic content: wrong role. We use AI to multiply what only we can make.

    ❌ If you want to manage a large team: we’d rather build the machine than grow the headcount.

    Help us market a product that fuses neuroscience, design, and AI to reinvent how humans grow.

    Build one of the first truly AI-native media, and write the playbook others will copy.

    Work with filmmakers, psychologists, engineers, and creatives obsessed with impact.

    You’ll compete with San Francisco companies.

    -> 🏅 Being surrounded by A-players who strive to perform.

    But you don’t just want a competitive paycheck, you also want….

    -> Playing a crucial role in the development of a tech giant whose content and products will be used by millions of people.

    -> Waking up in the morning feeling like you are making a difference is something!

    We receive messages every day from clients who have successfully lost weight, quit smoking, reached a milestone in their business, built better relationships, and made positive changes in their lives.

    But that’s not all, we believe that driven people deserve….

    -> 😎 A firm culture based on autonomy & accountability.

    -> 🗽 Flexible working hours (but very hard working).

    -> 🌎 A remote culture from day one with the freedom to work from wherever you want.

    -> 🧍‍♀️ Standing desks paid by the organization if you live far from our offices.

    -> 💻 Work on Mac, for us it counts :).

    -> 🏀 350€ per year paid by the manufacturer to take care of yourself (for your gym, or dance class or whatever make you feel great).

    -> 📚 150€ of books or education - At Paradox, we are learner lovers and we want to support you in that.

    -> 🔥 Access to Athena - our Paradox AI Coach supporting you on anything personal or professional, we want you to live your best life.

    In a recent development, ⚠️ To complete the recruitment process, each candidate must organize calls with his or her previous managers. If you are not comfortable with this : do not apply ⚠️.

    If all this sounds good to you, come and write the next chapter with us 🚀🚀🚀🚀.

    That job description resonated with you?

    Here is your tailor made hiring process.

    📃 A 6 to 8 minutes application survey, with links to content you made and something you built with AI.

    💻 A 30mn video call with Timy, HR, to deep dive into your career path and ambitions.

    💻 A 1h video call, to discuss how you’d fit into Paradox’s content team.

    💻 A 1h culture-fit video call, to assess alignment with our values and mindset.

    💻 A 1h final video call with David, CEO, to discuss the creative vision and the next milestones to build.

    💼 Reference check to understand how you operate across environments and help set you up for a smooth onboarding.

    Our recruitment process is tailored to do our best to avoid that you or us realize that we’re not a perfect fit. Every step serves a purpose and will allow us to get to know you better as much as it’ll help you understand more where you’ll be stepping in.

    We also want you to have time to ask all of your questions regarding the mission, the long-term vision of your team and the company, our values, with the relevant interlocutor in front of you.

    If you’re not joining to post content.

    If you’re here to build a media that changes how millions of people grow.

    Let’s build the Operating System for Greatness.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
    • We’re looking for a senior product designer to be the first dedicated designer on our product growth team, shaping how creators get set up, see value in their first days, and enjoy a seamless upgrade experience.
    • In a recent development, product growth is a fresh team at Kit, formed earlier this year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    We’re looking for a senior product designer to be the first dedicated designer on our product growth team, shaping how creators get set up, see value in their first days, and enjoy a seamless upgrade experience. Kit ships fast, and the product growth team builds the frameworks and systems that connect creators to the value in their plan as the product keeps changing. We need a designer who can balance rapid experimentation with long-term value for our creators.

    In a recent development, product growth is a fresh team at Kit, formed earlier this year. In the six months since, we’ve found our rhythm and started to move the numbers, but we’re still shaping how we work, how we prioritise and where we focus in the long term. As the team’s designer, you’ll be the design voice for growth, with real influence over how the team works and what it builds.

    Recent findings suggest that you'll own the design of the moments that move our funnel: onboarding, activation, free trials, upgrade and upsell flows, pricing and checkout, and billing. You'll work in a team that learns by shipping, through A/B tests and ship-and-measure changes, and you'll use data to decide what to try next.

    This is a full-time IC role for a designer who loves connecting design decisions to numbers, moves quickly without sacrificing quality, and is excited about using AI to accelerate outcomes.

    We need someone who thinks deeply about user behaviour, interaction design and the product experience, and who is proactive about finding the next opportunity rather than waiting for a spec.

    According to recent reports, you'll report to Dan Winer, Director of Product Design, and join a small, high-impact product design team at the moment consisting of four senior product designers and a senior design engineer. From day one, you’ll be part of the product growth team’s product trio alongside the product manager and engineering manager, shaping the team’s vision, priorities and how we work. You’ll also work closely with the team’s engineers.

    According to recent reports, first week: Get to know Kit’s product and the product growth team’s goals. Get access to Figma, Linear, Mixpanel and our other reporting tools. Take part in get-to-know-you calls with the team.

    It has been revealed that first month: Get up to speed on how we track and measure creator behaviour in Mixpanel, Omni and Clarity, which experiments are running now, and what we’ve learnt from past ones. Join the product trio’s planning and prioritisation discussions, and ship a small experiment or two, with support from the Director of Product Design as you take ownership of the growth work.

    In a recent development, first six months: Own design across the team’s work, which spans growth (onboarding, activation, trials and upgrades) and billing (checkout, plan changes, downgrades and cancellation). This might include personalising onboarding, improving free-to-paid conversion or simplifying our payment flows. By six months, the team should rely on you for a clear picture of how creators move through these flows, where they get stuck and why. You’ll help the team run more and better experiments, from forming a hypothesis to reading the results. We don’t have dedicated researchers, so you’ll talk to creators, run usability tests, track the impact of your work and proactively suggest iterations.

    First year: Help the team improve our activation, free-to-paid, trial conversion, and early retention rates, so that more creators upgrade, stay on Kit, and find real value. Turn our upsell, discount and plan change moments into one coherent experience instead of a set of one-off prompts.

    Interaction design for complex web applications, with a strong eye for visual hierarchy and detail.

    Grounding design decisions in the creator’s voice through interviews, usability testing and customer feedback, partnering with the PM so it shapes what we build as well as how.

    Designing flows that change depending on who’s seeing them, like free, trial and paid accounts, or creators upgrading and downgrading.

    Designing onboarding, activation, upgrade, pricing, checkout or billing flows.

    Experiment design and reading results, including knowing when an A/B test is the right approach or when to just ship and track.

    Defining what events to track so the team can measure what you shipped, using tools like Mixpanel.

    Clear written and visual communication of design rationale, including async walkthroughs.

    Around 5+ years as a product designer on SaaS or other complex web-based products.

    Led design on growth, monetisation or onboarding work and can point to its impact on metrics, ideally including retention or quality of conversion, not just volume.

    Worked in a cross-functional team with a product manager and engineers, shipping continuously.

    Worked within and contributed to an established design system.

    A portfolio that reveals how research or data informed your decisions and what happened as a result.

    Bonus: designed pricing, billing or proposal change experiences.

    Curious about why consumers behave the way they do, and about what the numbers aren’t telling you.

    Comfortable being wrong in public and sharing what you don’t know, not just what you do.

    Proactive and self-directed, with a bias for shipping.

    Excited about AI and pragmatic about how to use it.

    Low ego and comfortable giving and receiving direct feedback.

    Preferring to execute designs handed down from a product manager.

    Treating a conversion win as the finish line, without checking whether those creators stay with Kit and find value.

    Wanting long, highly-refined projects with little contact with data or results.

    Discomfort with experiments that fail or with changing direction based on what we learn.

    Focusing on visual polish without deeper thinking about user behaviour and business outcomes.

    Being philosophically opposed to using AI in your work.

    Needing well-established processes and a fully defined roadmap from day one.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time - so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Recent findings suggest that kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we're hiring at level 4 ($172,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance prepares through Aetna.

    According to recent reports, $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Company-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    It has been revealed that winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    Skydance’s Rebecca Mall Introduces Fresh Marketing Leadership Team

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that skydance’s marketing division is the latest unit to reveal its new leadership structure.
    • Recent findings suggest that chief marketing officer Rebecca Mall, in a memo to her team, confirmed the new vision for the marketing team.
    • She added that the team’s job is not just to market what they create, but also to help drive growth and success for the entire Skydance organization.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that skydance’s marketing division is the latest unit to reveal its new leadership structure. Following its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery in October, Skydance has been busy working to mesh the operations of the two media companies.

    Recent findings suggest that chief marketing officer Rebecca Mall, in a memo to her team, confirmed the new vision for the marketing team. “We have an incredible opportunity to build a more unified, innovative and effective marketing organization – one that breaks down silos, understands our audiences better than anyone and harnesses the power of creativity, data and technology to set a new standard for our industry,” according to the memo.

    She added that the team’s job is not just to market what they create, but also to help drive growth and success for the entire Skydance organization.

    Mall revealed that cross-company marketing and corporate brand, data & analytics, media, partnerships, and franchise and kids & family will now be housed under one roof. The new leadership team includes Annah Zafrani, who will be tasked with leading Skydance’s cross-company marketing and brand unit. Zafrani, who comes from Paramount Skydance, will coordinate priority campaigns across the media company’s businesses and lead corporate brand marketing. Reporting to her will be, also from the Paramount Skydance side, Katie Hutchings, svp, brand marketing, creative and strategy, and her team.

    Paramount Skydance’s Angie Sharma will lead franchise and kids & family, building one plan per franchise across content, consumer products, games, and experiences, with kids & family viewed as a key growth priority.

    According to recent reports, jamal Salmon, who comes from Paramount Skydance, will lead data & analytics for marketing, and will also report to Josh Goldstine, president of worldwide marketing & distribution, who will also be responsible for film marketing. Salmon will also have a dotted line to Hugh Williams, chief engineer and evp for consumer and monetization engineering; and Josh Walker, chief financial and strategy officer for direct to consumer. The DTC unit oversees streaming and video-on-demand.

    Sources indicate that paramount Skydance’s Michelle Hagen will lead brand partnerships, with Julie Moore, evp of brand partnerships, reporting to her, and Dana Nussbaum, co-head of global motion pictures marketing, Warner Bros., focusing on theatrical. Malene Sam, svp, originals, who was part of Paramount Skydance, report both to Hagen and Shauna Spenley, who leads DTC media. Under Spenley, Sam will be focused on TV and DTC.

    Industry observers note that finally, Seth Goren, who comes from WBD, will lead media, bringing together media strategy, media buying, and agency management across the company. He will report to Mall. But for theatrical media work, he also will report to Nussbaum. For his DTC media work, he will report to Spenley, and for his TV work, he will have a reporting line to Mike Benson, who leads TV Marketing.

    The realignment of the marketing team has led to the departure of Meg Maro, the global head of franchise. Mall thanked her for her contributions during her time at the company.

    Maro concluded saying: “We have an extraordinary opportunity to redefine what marketing can achieve in our industry, and I can’t wait to see what we accomplish together.”.

    Sources indicate that mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of Upcoming York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

You’ll own the deployment journey from first process file to a working, improving system, and hand off a functioning capability to the customer’s team. The code you write and the patterns you discover feed directly back into how ProcessOS is built. This is a rare opportunity to shape a product, a function, and a field practice from day one.

    You’ll work end‑to‑end across Java services and React interfaces, collaborating closely with a talented global team to measure, improve, and scale performance and fault tolerance in real-world distributed systems.

    Deploy and prove. Own the journey from first process file to production workflow. At 90 days: at least one workflow running, the improvement loop active, and measurable fitness gains the customer can see. At 12 months: 3–5 customers with viable deployments.

    Drive organizational adoption. Work across technical and business stakeholders to build understanding and trust, turning early deployments into lasting customer capability.

    According to recent reports, work at depth technically. Configure and run Camunda clusters locally and in cloud environments. Debug integration failures. Build custom agents where platform defaults don’t fit. Write connector logic that gets legacy enterprise systems talking to ProcessOS.

    Build the playbook. There is no deployment template yet. Document what good looks like as you discover it, and make the next implementation faster.

    Sources indicate that feed the product. Custom integrations you write get contributed back. Integration patterns get codified. Production bugs you find, you often fix. Your field work is a direct input to ProcessOS.

    Hand off deliberately. Leave customers with a team that can operate independently, is trained on the platform, and acts on improvement results without you.

    Ability and/or willingness to use our product.

    Recent findings suggest that enterprise production experience: you’ve shipped something inside a large organization and stayed to see it operate. You know why governance and resilience matter at scale.

    Technical depth: You can debug an integration failure, write a custom agent against a legacy API, stand up a Camunda cluster from scratch, and explain generated BPMN to both engineers and business leads.

    Stakeholder communication: you work effectively across engineering, architecture, and business leadership and adapt how you communicate without losing precision.

    According to recent reports, practical AI experience: you’ve used AI to solve real problems in production – not just experimented. You understand context management, prompt engineering, agent testing, and integration tradeoffs.

    Comfort with ambiguity: you make sound judgment calls without a playbook and document what you learn.

    Occasional travel may be required.

    Experience in a customer-facing engineering or professional services role.

    Familiarity with regulated industries such as financial services, healthcare, or insurance.

    Production experience with agentic systems or AI-integrated workflows.

    Contributions to a shared platform or open source project that others built on.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause.
    • According to recent reports, we are seeking a detail-oriented QA Specialist to ensure that every email and SMS campaign and journey is configured correctly and functions as intended prior to launch.
    • Conduct QA on all email and SMS campaigns and journeys in Iterable prior to launch to ensure every element is configured correctly and functions as intended.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Winona is one of the leading telemedicine companies providing HRT for women in menopause. We’ve built all of our technology in-house including an EHR, patient care admin system, patient portal, website, marketing technology etc. Winona has two compounding pharmacies and a team of in-house physicians providing world-class care via a fully vertically integrated business model.

    According to recent reports, we are seeking a detail-oriented QA Specialist to ensure that every email and SMS campaign and journey is configured correctly and functions as intended prior to launch. This role spans campaign configuration and tracking, content and design review, and cross-platform QA — identifying and resolving problems before they reach our audience.

    Seniority Level: Junior–Mid Level.

    Conduct QA on all email and SMS campaigns and journeys in Iterable prior to launch to ensure every element is configured correctly and functions as intended.

    Verify campaign and journey names against Winona’s naming conventions (name, year, event, medium and audience).

    Review journey configuration, including start tiles, suppressions, scheduled send dates and times, tile logic and conditionals, entry limits, exit rules and journey event tracking.

    Confirm that monthly and recurring journeys are refreshed with updated start tiles prior to each send.

    Verify that campaign labels are applied correctly (audience, segments, category, goal and month/year).

    Confirm that the appropriate conversion events are assigned for each campaign type: prospect, customer upsell, Shop, community and live event campaigns.

    Review delivery settings, including quiet hours, send time optimization, frequency caps and performance alerts.

    Verify that link tracking is configured correctly, including Google Analytics, UTM parameters and custom link parameters.

    Review sender details: message type, from name, from email and reply-to address.

    Review email templates against Winona’s brand and design standards, including fonts, sizing, padding, CTA button styling, link formatting and footers.

    Test all links, CTA buttons and image links, and confirm that images include alt text.

    Proofread copy for accuracy, consistency and formatting.

    Send and review test proofs in light and dark mode on iOS and Android, across both Gmail and Apple Mail.

    Coordinate SMS test sends with the appropriate team members prior to testing.

    Conduct QA on email touchpoints that connect to Shopify, such as Shop campaigns and checkout-related flows, to ensure a seamless end-to-end experience.

    Follow and help maintain internal templating documentation, QA checklists and the HTML template library.

    Communicate complications, errors and inconsistencies to the lifecycle team clearly and promptly, and track them through resolution.

    Recommend improvements to QA processes and standards on an ongoing basis.

    At least 3 years of experience performing QA within an ESP like Iterable or similar platforms.

    Working knowledge of HTML and CSS for email.

    Exceptional attention to detail and consistent checklist execution.

    Understanding of how emails render across clients, devices and dark mode.

    Clear written communication for reporting issues.

    Proficiency with Handlebars or dynamic content personalization.

    Shopify experience, particularly with checkout and order flows.

    Experience with email testing tools such as Litmus or Email on Acid.

    Familiarity with Google Analytics and UTM tracking.

    Experience with ClickUp or similar project management tools.

    Knowledge of SMS best practices and compliance standards (CAN-SPAM, CASL).

    As a full-time independent contractor, you’ll enjoy:.

    Remote-first, work wherever you choose.

    Paid non-working holidays per country of residence.

    Pro-rated 13th-month bonus in select regions.

    Financial support for online courses.

    Fun and casual work environment.

    Employee engagement activities and virtual gatherings.

    Sources indicate that we are a diverse, global team! 🌍.

    The Art, Science and Theater of Modern Marketing ft. Thomas Ranese

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • What if the best marketing advantage you have is something that cannot be replicated by an algorithm?
    • For Thomas Ranese, CMO of Intuit, it starts with theater, empathy and understanding what people are actually trying to achieve.
    • In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney sits down with Thomas to unpack how an unconventional career spanning theater, Google and Uber shaped his approach to marketing leadership.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What if the best marketing advantage you have is something that cannot be replicated by an algorithm?

    For Thomas Ranese, CMO of Intuit, it starts with theater, empathy and understanding what people are actually trying to achieve.

    In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney sits down with Thomas to unpack how an unconventional career spanning theater, Google and Uber shaped his approach to marketing leadership.

    From growing up behind the counter of his father’s pasta shop to leading marketing at one of the world’s biggest financial technology platforms, Thomas gets into why emotional connection can be just as powerful as performance data.

    He also addresses why AI needs human expertise to earn customer trust, and why brands should bring more humanity, creativity, and purpose into modern marketing.

    Thomas Ranese is Chief Marketing Officer at Intuit, a global technology platform serving millions of customers worldwide with TurboTax, QuickBooks, Credit Karma and Mailchimp.

    Sources indicate that his career has taken him through some very different worlds, including theater, consulting, government and nonprofit work, Google and Uber. His approach to marketing is rooted in a simple idea: understand what people are trying to achieve, then build brands and experiences that help them get there. He strongly believes in storytelling and using humor to make complex information more relatable.

    At Intuit, Thomas is helping shape the company’s evolution into an integrated, AI-powered financial technology platform, with a focus on combining technology with human expertise to help consumers and businesses prosper.

    Industry observers note that 07:18 Marketing Is Theater, and It Goes Beyond Advertising — Thomas breaks down the three different kinds of theater that shape modern marketing: the storytelling and drama of advertising, the emotions and interactions built into customer experience, and the immersive experiences brands create through retail. He also believes real-world human interactions will become increasingly key as more of our lives move into digital and AI-powered environments.

    Sources indicate that 12:44 What a Pasta Shop Taught Him About Customer Obsession — Thomas traces his interest in marketing back to his childhood, when he spent time working in his father’s small pasta shop. He loved being behind the counter, helping customers and figuring out what they needed. He even created his father’s first promotional newsletter on a Commodore 64. Looking back, he sees those early experiences as the foundation of his approach to customer connection, communication and service.

    16:01 Why AI Needs Human Intelligence Too — Intuit is building AI into the core of its financial technology platform, but Thomas is particularly focused on the role human experts play alongside it. When customers are making important decisions about taxes, credit or their businesses, getting the right answer matters. AI can provide powerful technology and efficiency, but human expertise brings verification, empathy and the confidence customers need to act.

    Sources indicate that 19:57 Money Is a Means to an End. So Is Your Product — Thomas challenges brands to think beyond what their products do and focus on what customers want to achieve with them. Small business owners aren’t necessarily starting businesses because they want to make money; they’re pursuing a craft, building a lifestyle, serving customers or creating opportunities for their families. The same principle applies across categories: brands become more meaningful when they understand the bigger ambitions their products help people achieve.

    Industry observers note that 22:00 Intuit’s Goal for Financial Literacy — Thomas explains how Intuit is connecting its mission to power prosperity with financial literacy education. Through Intuit for Education, the organization aims to reach 50 million students by 2030, addressing the fact that only 32% of students graduate able to pass a basic financial literacy exam. For Thomas, this is an opportunity to create meaningful social impact while building trust and introducing a newly introduced generation to the tools that can help them succeed.

    26:02 Why CMOs Should be Fully Involved — Thomas pushes back on the idea that senior marketing leaders should step away from execution as their organizations grow. With technology and AI changing marketing so rapidly, he believes CMOs need to stay hands-on, understand the tools and continue learning. He argues that the bigger the organization, the more notable this becomes, especially when it is easy to become disconnected from the actual work and the customers being served.

    Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.

    The Media RFP Is Quietly Becoming Obsolete ft. Bruce Williams

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Media used to be one part of the marketing machine, but this approach became outdated a while ago.
    • In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney sits down with Bruce Williams, CEO of dentsu X North America, to examine how media is becoming the connective tissue across creative, commerce, CRM, data, and technology.
    • Bruce reveals why standalone media RFPs are disappearing, and what it really takes to design connected consumer experiences.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Media used to be one part of the marketing machine, but this approach became outdated a while ago.

    In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney sits down with Bruce Williams, CEO of dentsu X North America, to examine how media is becoming the connective tissue across creative, commerce, CRM, data, and technology.

    Bruce reveals why standalone media RFPs are disappearing, and what it really takes to design connected consumer experiences.

    He also addresses why brands need to move from channel-first planning toward operating systems built around outcomes.

    Bruce Williams is CEO of dentsu X North America. Here, his focus is increasingly on helping brands move beyond isolated media planning toward connected operating models that bring together data, content, technology and consumer experience.

    With more than 20 years in media, Bruce has spent much of his career working at the intersection of media strategy, integrated marketing, technology and organizational transformation.

    He also works with clients on AI-enabled transformation, agency interoperability and latest ways to turn data into faster decision-making at both global and local levels.

    01:26 The “Media RFP” Is Quietly Becoming Obsolete — Bruce indicates media RFPs rarely arrive as standalone asks anymore. Brands increasingly want integrated briefs that connect media with creative, experience, CRM and loyalty, or they want agencies to solve bigger transformation problems. So, the agency conversation has to shift from “Can you buy media well?” to “Can you help us operate better?”.

    According to recent reports, 03:13 Your Customer Doesn’t Experience Your Brand in Silos — Marketing may still be organized into separate teams, systems and channels, but the person receiving the experience does not care about those distinctions. Bruce argues that fragmentation remains one of the industry’s longest-running problems because disconnected structures eventually show up as disconnected consumer experiences.

    Industry observers note that 06:22 On AI: Build the System, Then Stay Scrappy — Bruce does not see AI transformation as a choice between massive infrastructure projects and quick tactical wins. He points to work with Heineken that combines long-term data and technology integration with practical tools like local intelligence agents that move competitive and market data directly into local decisions.

    08:51 Why Agencies Can’t Keep Saying “Our Way or Nothing” — For Bruce, the future of agency relationships comes down to interoperability and optionality. Closed systems create friction. Agencies need to work directly with brand data, technology and other partners instead of expecting clients to conform to one proprietary model. Openness is becoming part of the value proposition.

    Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.
